```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r packages, message=FALSE}
library("naboer")
library("tibble")

have_ape <- requireNamespace("ape", quietly = TRUE)
have_rsample <- requireNamespace("rsample", quietly = TRUE)

if (have_ape) {
  library("ape")
}
if (have_rsample) {
  library("rsample")
}
```

Choose what to hold out based on where you want to make predictions. For
example, to assess predictions at a new station, fit the model without any of
that station's observations. You can also hold out observations from an
unfamiliar environment or from taxa that the model has never seen. When the
aim is to assess a particular observation while allowing for dependence among
nearby observations, use a buffer around it. The buffer excludes observations
from fitting while leaving the set of observations you score unchanged.

Start with a monitoring dataset of six stations across two networks. Each
station has four daily observations and its own temperature and moisture
measurements, which are constant across the four days in this example.

```{r monitoring-data}
observations <- tibble(
  observation = seq_len(24),
  network = rep(c("north", "south"), each = 12),
  station = rep(paste0("station", seq_len(6)), each = 4),
  date = rep(as.Date("2025-05-01") + 0:3, 6),
  temperature = rep(c(4, 6, 12, 14, 20, 22), each = 4),
  moisture = rep(c(90, 85, 65, 60, 35, 30), each = 4),
  habitat = rep(
    c("wet", "wet", "intermediate", "intermediate", "dry", "dry"), each = 4
  )
)
```

## Whole stations and hierarchical groups

Use `group_folds()` to leave out one station at a time. Selecting both
`network` and `station` makes the pair the group identifier. This also works
when different networks use the same station names.

```{r leave-one-station-out}
new_station <- observations |>
  group_folds(group = c(network, station), id = observation)
```

The summary shows six folds, each assessing four observations. Use
`assessment_indices()` to see which rows contribute to the error in a fold.
The indices are positions in the original table.

```{r inspect-station-folds}
as_tibble(new_station)
assessment_indices(new_station, folds = 1)
```

To assess multiple stations in each fold, set `v` to the number of folds.
The stations stay whole, and `balance = TRUE` aims to give the folds similar
numbers of observations. Setting `seed` makes this allocation reproducible
without changing your session's random number state.

```{r allocate-station-folds}
station_vfold <- observations |>
  group_folds(group = c(network, station), v = 3, balance = TRUE, seed = 21)
as_tibble(station_vfold)
```

Use `group = network` if the prediction target is a new network. If the
networks are independent for the purpose of defining groups or adding buffers,
use `.by = network`. This keeps group boundaries and buffers within networks.
When you request a set number of folds with `v`, a fold can still assess whole
groups from several networks.

## New environmental conditions

To assess predictions under unfamiliar conditions, use `environmental_folds()`
to hold out observations with similar predictor values. Here `v = 3` asks
k-means to form three clusters from temperature and moisture. The function
standardises each predictor to unit standard deviation by default, so the
distance calculation uses a common scale for both. Each cluster forms one
fold, and clusters can differ in size.

```{r cluster-environments}
new_environment <- observations |>
  environmental_folds(predictors = c(temperature, moisture), v = 3, seed = 22)
as_tibble(new_environment)
```

Choose predictors that describe the environmental differences you want to test.
Supply finite numeric values for each predictor. The function reports and
drops constant predictors. It needs at least one varying predictor and at
least `v` distinct combinations of predictor values. If you supply `.by`,
these checks and the clustering apply separately within each domain, with
`v` clusters in each.

If you already have environmental categories, supply them through `strata`.
This example assesses wet, intermediate and dry habitats in turn. To combine
whole habitats into fewer folds, supply `v`. In that case, `balance` controls
whether allocation balances the number of observations or the number of
habitats.

```{r leave-one-habitat-out}
new_habitat <- observations |>
  environmental_folds(strata = habitat)
as_tibble(new_habitat)
```

These folds may require predictions outside the range of conditions seen in
training. If predictor values change over time at a station, clustering can
put its observations in different folds. When you need to keep stations
together, use categories that are constant within each station. If you want
only to exclude nearby observations from fitting, add a buffer to the folds.

## Phylogenetic dependence and new taxa

These examples run when the optional `ape` package is installed. Use it to make
a tree of four taxa, then create a table with six observations per taxon. All
observed taxa must match tip labels in the tree, and each branch needs a finite,
non-negative length. The tree may include unused tips.

```{r tree-and-observations, eval=have_ape}
tree <- read.tree(
  text = "((oak:1,beech:1):2,(pine:1,fir:1):2);"
)
taxon_data <- tibble(
  observation = seq_len(24),
  taxon = rep(c("oak", "beech", "pine", "fir"), each = 6)
)
```

Tree distance is the sum of branch lengths along the path between two taxa.
Oak and beech are two units apart, and oak and pine are six units apart. To
assess one observation at a time while excluding its close relatives from
training, set a radius in those same units. A radius of two includes taxa
exactly two units away.

```{r phylogenetic-neighbourhoods, eval=have_ape}
near_taxa <- taxon_data |>
  neighbourhoods(
    phylogenetic = phylogenetic_window(tree, taxon, radius = 2),
    id = observation
  )
```

Inspect the first fold. It scores the first oak observation and leaves all oak
and beech observations out of the fit. The exclusion applies within the same
domain when you use `.by`. The function calculates distances once between taxa
and reuses them across observations of each taxon.

```{r inspect-phylogenetic-neighbourhood, eval=have_ape}
assessment_indices(near_taxa, folds = 1)
omitted <- omission_indices(near_taxa, folds = 1)[[1]]
unique(taxon_data$taxon[omitted])
```

To assess all observations from a group of taxa together, use
`phylogenetic_folds()`. Supply `v` for a set number of groups or `height` for
a maximum distance between any pair of taxa in a group. Here `height = 2`
groups oak with beech and pine with fir. All observations of the held-out taxa
are scored.

```{r phylogenetic-blocks, eval=have_ape}
taxon_blocks <- taxon_data |>
  phylogenetic_folds(tree, taxon, height = 2)
as_tibble(taxon_blocks)
```

If you use `.by`, a fold holds out a group within one domain, and the same
taxon can remain in training in another. Leave `.by` unspecified to assess
taxa that are absent from the entire training dataset.

You can also define the groups directly from branches of a rooted tree. Supply
the node number or the complete set of descendant tip labels for each clade.
The clades must cover every observed taxon, and each tip can belong to only
one selected clade. Here we specify the two pairs explicitly.

```{r phylogenetic-clades, eval=have_ape}
new_clade <- taxon_data |>
  phylogenetic_folds(
    tree, taxon,
    clades = list(c("oak", "beech"), c("pine", "fir"))
  )
as_tibble(new_clade)
```

## Buffered resampling and rsample

Start with leave-one-out folds for the monitoring data. Each observation is
scored in its own fold.

```{r focal-design}
leave_one_out <- loo_folds(observations, id = observation)
```

Add a one-day buffer around the assessment observation in each fold. With
`key = station` and `within = "key"`, the buffer stays within the same
station. Distances are measured from the assessment observation itself.

```{r buffered-design}
buffered <- buffer_folds(
  leave_one_out,
  temporal = temporal_window(time_span(1, "days")),
  key = station, index = date, within = "key"
)
```

In fold 2, row 2 is still the only assessment observation. The buffer also
excludes rows 1 and 3 from fitting, so `n_buffer` is 2 and the analysis set
starts at row 4.

```{r inspect-buffered-fold}
as_tibble(buffered, folds = 2)
analysis_indices(buffered, folds = 2)
```

The next examples require the optional **rsample** package. Export with
`as_rset()` to refit the model on each analysis set using rsample. The
exported resamples store the analysis and assessment sets separately. Rows
excluded by the buffer alone belong to neither set.

```{r export-rsample, eval=have_rsample}
resamples <- as_rset(buffered)
```

Import with `from_rset()` to get a naboer design back. It treats all rows
outside the analysis set as omitted, so the buffer survives the round trip.
These comparisons check all three sets.

```{r rsample-roundtrip, eval=have_rsample}
restored <- from_rset(resamples)
identical(assessment_indices(restored), assessment_indices(buffered))
identical(omission_indices(restored), omission_indices(buffered))
identical(analysis_indices(restored), analysis_indices(buffered))
```

The export also saves which columns hold series keys, time indices, domains
and observation identifiers. Import restores those selections for use in later
operations. For resamples created elsewhere, supply `key`, `index`, `.by` and
`id` as needed. Explicit selections take precedence over saved ones.

You can import ordinary and repeated V-fold resamples. The splits must all
refer to the same data in the same row order, and each analysis set must
contain unique rows. Bootstrap samples that repeat a row cannot be represented
by this design.

Create resamples on individual observation rows. With a nested spatial cubble,
use the cubble package's `face_temporal()` to switch to one row per observation,
or resample the observation table returned by `fold_data()`. If a row
represents an entire station, its index cannot identify a single observation
after expansion.

Exporting to rsample can take much more memory than storing a naboer design.
For example, leave-one-out stores almost all row indices in each rsample
analysis set. `as_rset()` estimates the memory needed for the analysis and
assessment indices before creating them. The default limit comes from
`getOption("naboer.max_bytes", 1024^3)`, and you can change it with `max_bytes`.
The estimate counts integer indices and excludes R object overhead.

For neighbourhood cross-validation in mgcv, pass `as_nei(buffered)` as `nei`
and fit to `fold_data(buffered)`. Prepare complete modelling data before
constructing folds and use `na.action = na.fail` when fitting. Check
whether the approximation is accurate for your model and omission size.
See [Assessment, omission and prediction targets](naboer.html) for an example.
